According to the latest issue of Mark Gurman's "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering multiple changes to its App Store. What's the goal? It's to increase the potential revenue that the App Store can generate.

The specifics of Apple's App Store overhaul remain unclear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the relevant work primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

According to reports, this overhaul was one of the reasons veteran employee Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020, transitioning to the role of Apple Fellow, at which time part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller disagreed with the related proposals:

Apple has many ways to improve App Store profit margins. For example, it could eliminate the manual app review process — in an era of automated coding, this procedure is costly and highly questionable. Further automating review could anger users, but would undoubtedly save money.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 per month subscribing to Codex and Claude to build apps, Apple is well-positioned to raise prices without facing too much resistance. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some infrastructure costs.

What the final outcome will be remains unknown, but I very much look forward to seeing what these changes ultimately look like.
